f: dry out under strong sun, using racks
sink below water, using weights
bury deep under ground, using a spade
r: Old English sundrian “to separate, split, part, divide”
s: In Taran's hand the sundered bone had turned into gray dust, which he cast aside.

f: sticky to the touch
quick to change direction
easily turned aside
r: Latin taciturnus, from tacitus “secret, tacit”
s: The two sisters could hardly have been more different, one so boisterous and expressive, the other so taciturn and calm.

f: remove the core from
drive out evil spirits
dig out by scooping
r: Late Latin excoriō “to take the skin or hide off”
s: The teacher continued to excoriate the student after his academic issues.

f: excessively careful (and often pointless) reasoning
compulsively frequent (and often secret) writing
chronically damaged (and often swollen) eyelids
r: logo- “word; speech” + -rrhea “flowing”
s: A volubility sometimes amounting to a logorrhœa in expressing what they know.

f: adapted for digging especially by scraping with broad flat feet
adapted for swimming especially by paddling with webbed toes
adapted for warning especially by producing a loud rattle
r: Latin prehēnsus, from prehendō “grasp, seize”
s: Some monkeys have prehensile tails which they use to pick things up.

f: someone who carries messages between two parties who refuse to meet in person
someone who runs away with a partner in order to marry without consent
someone who measures land and marks its boundaries for a title deed
r: inter- + loper “runner, rover”
s: They disliked the interloper, and forced him to leave.

f: a woman who campaigned for the right to vote
a long hymn sung on days of fasting
a minor clerk who keeps parish records
r: Old French suffragan, from Latin suffrāgium “suffrage”
s: A suffragan could share the tasks which were special to bishops; for example, by conducting confirmations.

f: standing on the hind legs with forepaws raised as if to strike
walking with the right forepaw raised and head turned to face the viewer
sitting upright on the haunches with the tail curled around the feet
r: Middle French couchant
s: Have you ever watched fine collie dogs couchant at twenty yards' distance?

f: cause to grow mold or decay; spoil by leaving in damp
grind into a fine powder; crush with a pestle
shape in a mold or cast; form from soft clay
r: Late Latin mollificō, from Latin mollis “soft”
s: He tried to mollify the angry customer.

f: eager for new experiences and not afraid of danger
arriving in time for a holiday and not a moment late
useful for some purpose and not just decoration
r: Medieval Latin adventītius “coming from abroad, extraneous”, from Latin adventus “arrival”
s: The adventitious disappearance of those nearer the throne than the duke had, moreover, set tongues awagging.

f: chat idly with neighbors
cook slowly on a skewer
wrap tightly in cloth
r: Origin uncertain; possibly a variant of kurbash “heavy whip, lash”
s: An Allied mission to kibosh the German A-bomb.

f: feelings of disgust that make you turn away from food
feelings of contentment that come after long hard work
feelings of loneliness that come from living in silence
r: dis- + quietude
s: The lawyer stood awhile when Mr. Hyde had left him, the picture of disquietude.

f: possessing or claiming to possess great skill especially in storytelling
relating to or made of soft white clay especially for medicine
tending to or inclined to gossip especially about neighbors
r: talisman + -ic
s: For Marshall, law possessed a talismanic quality, representing all that was best in American democracy.

f: someone who seizes a throne without any rightful claim to it
someone who guides guests to their seats at a theatre
someone who repairs worn-out tools and household goods for resale
r: Old French usurier, from Latin ūsūra “interest”
s: You can go to the Carpetbag usurers if you want money.

f: a pole for measuring the depth of a channel or harbor
a yard of land set aside for grazing horses or cattle
a hook for hauling fish or nets onto a boat
r: Middle English halier, from halen “to haul”, later confused with yard
s: Uncleat the black main halyard to lower and remove the jib cover.

f: a slanting line used in writing
a formal speech praising the dead
a duty imposed by law or custom
r: Late Latin obloquium “contradiction”, from Latin obloquor “speak against”
s: The death of her honour has added obloquy and shame to that sorrow which bends my grey hairs to the dust!

f: open and easy to reach
thick and cloudy
hopeful about the future
r: Latin opulēns, from ops “wealth, power, resources”
s: Bowed into the opulent suites of Ritzes and Waldorfs.

f: of fine grain; smooth and polished
of great age; worn and wrinkled
of noble birth; proud and stately
r: Latin elephantīnus; elephant + -ine
s: Overhead and all around came the elephantine sounds of hundreds of students on the move.

f: the loose sand on a riverbed
the small boats of a fleet
the froth that forms on beer
r: Anglo-Norman floteson, from Old French flotaison “a floating”
s: That gaggle of human flotsam doesn't even belong on the sea.

f: iron or wooden frame for a saddle, with a horn for roping
leather or felt pad for a horse, with a pocket for oats
clay or stone trough for a stable, with a spout for draining
r: Perhaps Spanish jáquima “halter”
s: He’d hauled the horse around by the hackamore and was pounding off up the track.

f: rough broom; made of a single bundle of twigs
thick broth; made with a single kind of meat
heavy boot; worn by a single class of laborer
r: Named after the British statesman Lord Brougham (1778–1868)
s: “A nice little brougham and a pair of beauties.”

f: the theory that all matter is made of a single substance
the sense of urgency that drives prophets to preach in public
the practice of composing hymns for performance at religious festivals
r: Greek theourgíā “sorcery”, from theós “god” + érgon “work”
s: Spiritual magic or theurgy was based on the idea that one could reach God in an ascent up the scale of creation.

f: easily erased or removed
reckless and impulsive
bright with rainbow colors
r: Late Latin īrāscibilis, from Latin īrāscī “to be angry, enraged”
s: I am naturally irascible, and if I could have shaken this negative gentleman vigorously, the relief would have been immense.

f: a pale beer brewed and stored at low temperatures
a wide flat field flooded for growing rice
a small cart drawn by a pair of dogs
r: South African Dutch lager “camp”, from German Lager; a doublet of lager and lair
s: Then our frontiers will shrink as we draw our little laager more and more tightly.

f: a small round shield that was carried by foot soldiers in the Middle Ages
a shallow iron pot that was used for cooking over open fires in the Middle Ages
a narrow strip of land that was farmed by peasants in the Middle Ages
r: Old English cyrtel; compare Old Norse kyrtill “tunic”
s: Many of the church dignitaries are distinguishable by peculiarities of dress, as the shovel hat and kirtle.

f: a large brass bell rung to call workers home
a member of a powerful family group
a metal latch on a farm gate
r: clang “loud ringing sound” + -er
s: In his speech, the best man got the bride's name wrong. What a clanger!

f: reading a meaning into dreams
planning a route before travel
comparing a text with its source
r: Greek prâxis “action, activity, practice”
s: Differences between theory and praxis of communism.

f: resembling or characteristic of a brother or sister
resembling or characteristic of a soft hissing sound
resembling or characteristic of a pale silver metal
r: Latin sibyllinus, from Sibylla; sibyl + -ine
s: Another early form of rhapsodomancy is represented by the sibylline books.

f: small round cake with a crust; for eating at weddings and feasts
tall narrow tower with a bell; for calling villagers to prayer
thick woollen cloth with a twill; for making coats and cloaks
r: French terrine; a doublet of terrine
s: The large covered soup tureen, as well as the 15 inch round plate on which it sat, was rimmed by gold leaf.

f: a person who speaks in roundabout phrases
a person who lives at the edge of a town
a person who preaches outdoors
r: Greek peripatētikós “given to walking around”, from perí “around” + patéō “to walk”
s: He who would think clearly must think like a peripatetic even if he is unwilling to walk like one.

f: prone to constant nagging
ground into a paste
ripe with summer fruit
r: Latin pestifer “bearing plague”, from pestis “plague” + -fer “carrying”
s: In these solemn moments man discovers the germ of those vices, which like the Java tree shed a pestiferous vapour around.

f: repeating the same sound at the start of several words in a line or phrase
placing two words of opposite meaning side by side for dramatic effect
describing something by stating what it is not in order to emphasize it
r: Greek sunekdokhḗ “receiving together”, from sún “with” + ek “out of” + dékhesthai “to accept”
s: "Holocaust" can become a tired synecdoche for war crimes in general.

f: shorten or cut off especially by trimming the ends
breathe out or release especially by sighing heavily
dig up or remove especially by digging around the roots
r: Latin exhortārī “to encourage”, from ex- + hortārī “to incite, spur”
s: And now, my dear sir, let me exhort you to take care of yourself.
